painpoints.title: Ten-year-old catalog architecture and an open rebuild question
painpoints.summary: The catalog was built about ten years ago by reverse-engineering retailer point-of-sale data, back when grocers had no e-commerce catalogs to send. That origin still shapes the structure, and people across catalog describe being stuck with legacy systems nobody wants to touch. Whether to rebuild from first principles or extend what exists is still open, and Brittany expects this PM, the engineering manager, and the ops manager to bring a proposal.
painpoints.why_it_matters: Sonali tied the legacy code directly to repeat incidents. Brittany framed 2027 planning around whether the current framework can scale, and a wrong call either way costs a year.

solutions.name: Stress-test the current model against named use cases
solutions.description: Write the hardest upcoming consumer use cases (agentic queries, allergen filters, household profiles, international) as executable test cases and score the current schema and pipelines against each. The rebuild decision becomes a gap list with a cost per gap.
solutions.precedent: Architecture fitness functions from Building Evolutionary Architectures (Ford, Parsons, Kua)

solutions.name: Strangler-fig migration by attribute family
solutions.description: Stand up a new attribute store beside the old one and move one family at a time, starting with allergens or health tags, with dual writes and a diff monitor until parity. The old path retires family by family with no big-bang cutover.
solutions.precedent: Martin Fowler's Strangler Fig pattern; Shopify's componentization of its Rails monolith (Shopify engineering blog, 2019)

solutions.name: Rebuild as a product knowledge graph with per-value provenance
solutions.description: Model the catalog as canonical products, offers, and attribute assertions, where every assertion carries source, time, confidence, and rights. Retailer POS rows become one evidence source feeding the graph.
solutions.precedent: Amazon Product Graph and AutoKnow (KDD 2020); DoorDash product knowledge graph built with LLMs (DoorDash engineering blog)

demonstrate.idea: A one-page rebuild decision memo with options to extend, strangle, or rebuild, each scored on cost, risk, and the use cases it unlocks, in the PM plus EM plus ops proposal format Brittany described.

Build the gluten-free evidence engine on a provenance-first schema (each claim stored as an assertion with source and timestamp), then show the same query answered from it and from a flat badge table.
A working mini product graph for about 1,000 grocery items merged from Open Food Facts, USDA FoodData Central, and the Kroger product API, with an MCP query layer an agent can call.

painpoints.title: Attribute demand is outgrowing the generation process
painpoints.summary: Every downstream team wants more attributes: search, replacements, health, meals, and now agents. Tarang said the way catalog comes up with and generates new attributes probably has to be completely rethought, from product definition through pipeline structure to running at scale with a quality bar. Brittany described today's process as time-consuming and prone to human error.
painpoints.why_it_matters: Tarang called supporting health and meals non-optional, so attribute generation sits on the critical path of company bets. If throughput stays manual, catalog becomes the bottleneck for Clementine and every partner agent.

sources.quote: if we had to solve for actually everything that consumers of catalog are hoping to get from catalog over the next couple of years, they just need a lot more catalog data.
sources.context: Mike asked which roadmap projects he was excited about. Labeled 'Them'; section header confirms Tarang.

sources.quote: the ways we have come up with how we even generate new attributes has to probably be, like, completely rethought.
sources.context: Same answer.

sources.quote: All the way from product definition to the process of then, like, coming up with a pipeline structure, then running the pipelines, and then, like, actually doing it at scale with the quality bar.
sources.context: Same answer, continued.

sources.quote: someone who understands data as a product and, and how that will scale with, like, agentic shopping, with these downstream teams wanting more and more data attributes.
sources.context: Mike asked what Brittany is looking for in this hire.

sources.quote: We're always trying to deliver more data to these downstream teams, like search, replacements, etc.
sources.context: What she looks for in a PM partner.

sources.quote: And the way that this process works today is time-consuming and also prone to human error.
sources.context: Mike asked about the first six months and the two-year outlook.

solutions.name: Standard attribute spec at intake
solutions.description: Every new attribute starts as a one-page spec: definition, consuming surfaces, precision and recall targets, sources, refresh cadence, and rights. Specs are triaged weekly so the queue and its value are visible.
solutions.precedent: Amazon Selling Partner API product type definitions (JSON Schema per product type); Akeneo PIM attribute families

solutions.name: Template library of pipeline archetypes
solutions.description: Most attributes fit a handful of patterns: claim extraction from label text, numeric extraction from nutrition panels, derived scores, and certification lookups. Ship each as a reusable template so a new attribute is mostly configuration plus a golden set.
solutions.precedent: Instacart PARSE (public tech blog, 2025) already lets non-engineers define attributes in a UI; dbt packages as a reuse model

solutions.name: Goal-to-pipeline agent
solutions.description: An agent takes a plain-language attribute goal, drafts the definition, proposes sources, drafts a golden set for human review, assembles the pipeline from templates, and reports measured precision and recall before anything publishes. Humans approve at two gates.
solutions.precedent: Instacart's open Engineering Manager, Catalog req describes autonomous pipeline construction from plain-language goals (research doc 02); DSPy prompt optimization (Stanford)

demonstrate.idea: Open the gluten-free demo with its attribute spec, then show a second attribute (dairy-free) reusing the same pipeline with only a new spec and gold set.
A throughput model of attributes requested versus shipped per quarter under today's process, templates, and an agent builder, with assumptions Mike can tune live.
A small agent that takes 'sesame-free' as a prompt and returns a spec, a source plan, a 50-item draft gold set, and measured precision on Open Food Facts data, end to end.

painpoints.title: Each enrichment pipeline is assembled by hand
painpoints.summary: Peggy's team builds hundreds of enrichment pipelines. For each one they gather inputs, pick a model, design audit steps, maybe use LLM-as-judge, and send uncertain items to a BPO for labeling. Tarang said they need the right tooling and platform underneath, and Peggy said investing in that tooling is how the team builds faster.
painpoints.why_it_matters: With hundreds of pipelines each carrying its own design choices, quality and cost vary by whoever built it. Tooling is the multiplier on a nine-person ops team.

sources.quote: I will then create the right audit steps. I'll maybe use testing using LLM as a judge, and then maybe I'll also send some stuff off to a BPO to then manually label, where I'm not sure.
sources.context: Describing how Peggy's team builds the gluten-free pipeline. Labeled 'Them'.

sources.quote: And now, for them to do that, they need the right tooling and platform, right?
sources.context: Same description, continued.

sources.quote: a really good PM partner balances those business needs with also the enablement or foundation needs as well because to build faster, we also have to invest in the tooling and how do we balance both those things.
sources.context: Mike asked what she looks for in a PM partner.

sources.quote: how do we actually support and build tools that our operations team can use to create that new information
sources.context: Describing the role. A charter statement more than a complaint, so a soft confirmation.

solutions.name: Pipeline scaffold with built-in evaluation gates
solutions.description: Every pipeline gets the same skeleton: input contract, model step, golden-set eval, judge step, human-review routing, and a publish gate that blocks output below the agreed precision. Builders fill in only what differs.
solutions.precedent: Write-Audit-Publish pattern (popularized by Netflix with Apache Iceberg); Great Expectations checkpoints

solutions.name: Shared model router
solutions.description: A central router picks the cheapest model that meets each attribute's measured quality bar and escalates hard cases to larger models or humans. Pipelines declare targets and the router decides.
solutions.precedent: FrugalGPT model cascades (Stanford, 2023); PARSE's published cascade result of 70 percent lower cost on simple attributes

solutions.name: Self-optimizing pipelines
solutions.description: Pipelines tune their own prompts and thresholds against the golden set on a schedule, and a human approves any change that moves metrics.
solutions.precedent: DSPy (Stanford); Amazon catalog's self-learning generative AI on Bedrock (AWS ML blog); Instacart's Agentic ML post on an agent revising extraction instructions

demonstrate.idea: Present the gluten-free engine as a pipeline with visible stages (sources, extraction, conflict check, gold-set eval, publish gate) and let the viewer switch a stage off to see quality change.
A pipeline linter that reads a pipeline config and flags a missing eval, refresh cadence, or rights metadata.
A no-code pipeline builder where an ops analyst composes the gluten-free pipeline from blocks and gets a precision and recall report before publishing.

painpoints.title: Deciding fast which source is accurate
painpoints.summary: Catalog data arrives from content service providers, retailer feeds, point of sale, and in-store shoppers, all at different quality levels. Brittany named making fast decisions on what is accurate at a given point in time as a core catalog challenge, and pressed on how to pick the right source when allergens need 99.5 percent precision. Peggy described detecting and fixing issues at scale across these inputs as half of her team's job.
painpoints.why_it_matters: Arbitration is where a wrong allergen value gets chosen over a right one, so it sets the precision ceiling for every downstream surface.

sources.quote: So one of the challenges that we have within the catalog space is how do you actually make sure that when you have data from all of these different sources, you're making fast decisions on what's actually accurate at that given point of time.
sources.context: Mike asked where catalog data comes from.

sources.quote: different sources, how would you determine what's the right source? Especially looking at allergens you're trying to hit 99.5% precision.
sources.context: Questioning Mike's proposed verification layer. Labeled 'Them'.

sources.quote: we have varying data inputs from different sources at different quality levels. How might we, like, detect issues at scale and also fix them at scale
sources.context: Overview of the catalog ops team.

solutions.name: Source hierarchy per attribute family
solutions.description: Write explicit precedence per family: certification wins for medical diet claims, the current label wins for allergens, CSP wins for nutrition, retailer wins for price. Conflicts route to review and are never silently resolved.
solutions.precedent: Instacart public docs name four prioritization methods and resolve alcohol conflicts to the most restrictive value; Mike's jam proposal

solutions.name: Freshness-aware arbitration
solutions.description: Weight evidence by age and by reformulation signals such as label photo dates and UPC changes. A two-year-old certification loses to a new label photo that contradicts it.
solutions.precedent: GS1 GDSN effective dates and change indicators; Open Food Facts photo timestamps

solutions.name: Learned source reliability
solutions.description: Estimate each source's accuracy per attribute family and category from audited samples, then combine evidence probabilistically. Sources that drift get down-weighted automatically.
solutions.precedent: Dawid-Skene annotator reliability model; Google's Knowledge-Based Trust truth discovery (Dong et al., VLDB 2015)

demonstrate.idea: The gluten-free engine itself: four sources, explicit precedence, a Conflict status when they disagree, and provenance on every claim.
Measure each source's precision against the hand-labeled gold set and show a source reliability table by category such as bread, snacks, and sauces.
Add Dawid-Skene style source weighting to the engine and show precision and coverage against fixed precedence at the same threshold.

painpoints.title: Allergen and medical diet tags need near-perfect precision
painpoints.summary: Brittany set the bar at 99 percent precision and recall for new attribute data, and 99.5 percent precision for allergens. Tarang said catalog cannot get tree-nut-free wrong. These are health claims where a miss can put someone in the hospital.
painpoints.why_it_matters: One wrong allergen badge is a safety event and a legal exposure, and it teaches the most loyal segment to distrust every badge.

sources.quote: what underlying data does it need for them to be able to hit a 99% precision and recall bar for that new data.
sources.context: Describing the role.

sources.quote: Especially looking at allergens you're trying to hit 99.5% precision.
sources.context: Questioning Mike's source selection logic. Labeled 'Them'.

sources.quote: especially for health, especially for, like, allergens, like, we cannot get tagging something tree nut free wrong.
sources.context: Roadmap excitement question. Labeled 'Them'.

solutions.name: Tiered claim statuses
solutions.description: Publish Verified only above the bar and show Claimed (a source asserts it and nobody has independently confirmed it) as a separate, clearly worded tier. Recall rises through the Claimed tier without spending Verified precision.
solutions.precedent: Mike's jam proposal; Amazon Climate Pledge Friendly uses third-party certifications as the badge basis

solutions.name: Certification-backed verification
solutions.description: For medical claims, require a matched certification or a current label read before Verified.
solutions.precedent: GFCO certified product directory; NSF gluten-free certification [VERIFY]

solutions.name: Calibrated abstention
solutions.description: Calibrate model confidence on the gold set and abstain below threshold, routing to humans. Conformal prediction gives a guaranteed error rate on what does publish.
solutions.precedent: Conformal prediction (Angelopoulos and Bates tutorial, 2021); selective classification

demonstrate.idea: The engine's precision and recall slider shows exactly how much coverage the team gives up to hold 99.5 percent precision on gluten-free.
Calibrate the LLM label reader's confidence on the gold set and plot a reliability diagram.
Add conformal abstention to the engine and report a guaranteed error rate on the published Verified set.

painpoints.title: No ground truth for generated health tags
painpoints.summary: Instacart generates its own health tags such as gluten-free and sesame-free, and Tarang said there is no ground truth data to ingest for them. Peggy's case question asked where to source data for a new attribute like GLP-1, internal or external, which is the same problem in a new form.
painpoints.why_it_matters: Without ground truth the 99.5 percent precision target cannot be measured, and any LLM-as-judge setup ends up grading against itself.

sources.quote: All those tags, we actually generate them ourselves. ... there's no ground truth data that we can just ingest to make that happen.
sources.context: Describing the Generated Content team. Labeled 'Them'; an em-dash stutter elided.

sources.quote: how would you think through, like, where to get that data from, right? Internal versus external.
sources.context: Posed as a case question about building a GLP-1 attribute, so it signals the problem without describing current state.

solutions.name: Hand-labeled golden set per attribute
solutions.description: Build a stratified gold set per attribute from label photos read by trained reviewers with double labeling and adjudication, and report inter-rater agreement.
solutions.precedent: Cohen's kappa; Mike's UARC2 expert-panel ground truth

solutions.name: External evidence as partial ground truth
solutions.description: Use certification registries and public datasets as evidence for subsets: GFCO certified products, USDA FoodData Central branded ingredients, Open Food Facts labels.
solutions.precedent: USDA FoodData Central Branded Foods (built with GS1 US, 1WorldSync, Label Insight, and NielsenIQ)

solutions.name: Active learning loop
solutions.description: Route the items where models disagree most to human labelers so each label buys the most precision, and grow the gold set where it matters.
solutions.precedent: Uncertainty-sampling active learning; Snorkel weak supervision; Label Studio

demonstrate.idea: Publish the 200-item hand-labeled gluten-free gold set with its labeling guide and agreement stats as part of the demo.
Count how many GFCO-certified products lack a gluten-free tag in the other sources, as an external-evidence coverage check.
Run an active-learning loop on the engine: label 50 more items chosen by disagreement and chart precision gained per label.

painpoints.title: Nobody can easily explain why an attribute value won
painpoints.summary: When an attribute ends up with a given value, tracing why is hard. Precedence is not linear across attributes or retailers, some retailers have contractual terms that promote their data, and Marketplace and Storefront Pro can differ for the same retailer. Internal tools now diagnose a product down to the source level, but documentation varies.
painpoints.why_it_matters: Explainability is the cost inside every escalation and every retailer question. Brittany called it absolutely a pain point and Peggy said the team faces the same issue.

sources.quote: It's absolutely a pain point. We have and I think the catalog was built 10 years ago.
sources.context: Mike asked whether diagnostics and explainability were a pain point for ops. Labeled 'Them'; section confirms Brittany.

sources.quote: Very much so. We, we face the same issue.
sources.context: Mike asked the same diagnostics question.

sources.quote: there's general confusion because, like, it's not linear across attributes and it's not linear across retailers.
sources.context: Same answer, continued.

sources.quote: even sometimes between marketplace and SFP for a particular retailer, it can be different. So that adds to the confusion.
sources.context: Same answer. SFP is Storefront Pro, the white-label product.

sources.quote: we have some, like, contractual obligations, right, with retailers where we, like, maybe promote more of their data, but that's not the same for, like, retailer B, right?
sources.context: Same answer, continued.

sources.quote: I think documentation varies.
sources.context: Mike asked about documentation quality.

solutions.name: Value lineage panel
solutions.description: For any product, retailer, and channel, show every candidate value with its source, timestamp, and the rule that picked the winner. Ops already has part of this; extend it to rule versions and contractual overrides.
solutions.precedent: Reltio MDM crosswalks showing contributing sources per attribute; Informatica MDM survivorship rules

solutions.name: Precedence rules as versioned configuration
solutions.description: Move source-priority logic out of code into a declarative rules table keyed by attribute family, retailer, and channel, with change history and tests. Explaining a value becomes reading a rule.
solutions.precedent: Open Policy Agent policy-as-code; Instacart's public docs already state per-attribute rules such as most-restrictive-wins for alcohol

solutions.name: Natural-language explanation service
solutions.description: An LLM reads lineage and the rule log and writes a cited plain-English explanation for ops, retailers, or downstream teams. The same service answers what would change if a retailer sent a different field.
solutions.precedent: Mike's Frida natural-language layer over UARC2 diagnostics (80 percent faster investigation); Stripe Radar risk insights [VERIFY]

demonstrate.idea: Every badge in the gluten-free engine opens a 'why' panel listing each source, its claim, its timestamp, and the rule that decided the status.
A rules-as-config prototype: a YAML precedence table for a few attribute families and both channels, with a test harness showing which source wins for sample products.
An explainer agent that answers 'why is this product gluten-free at retailer A and not at retailer B' from lineage data, with citations.

painpoints.title: Downstream teams cannot tell what an attribute means or whether to trust it
painpoints.summary: Catalog has rich data, but teams outside catalog see many fields with no built-in guidance on meaning, quality, freshness, or intended use. Peggy called a better semantic layer the thing she is most excited for in 2027. Brittany suspects some downstream teams use attributes incorrectly because they do not know how they are supposed to.
painpoints.why_it_matters: Misused attributes produce customer-facing errors that look like catalog defects. A semantic layer also speeds the use, test, and feedback loop Peggy wants with downstream teams.

sources.quote: we don't do a great job of this today on how we might build a better semantic layer for all of our downstream teams
sources.context: Mike asked about the biggest technology opportunity for 2027.

sources.quote: there's lots of, like, data fields, a lot of, like, attributes, and they don't know what is this data? Should I use it or should I not use it?
sources.context: Same answer, continued.

sources.quote: What's the quality? What is the freshness?
sources.context: Same answer, continued.

sources.quote: maybe one of the challenges is that they are just using the attributes that we deliver incorrectly 'cause they just don't know how they're supposed to.
sources.context: Mike asked what a semantic layer looks like to her.

solutions.name: Data product card per attribute
solutions.description: Each attribute ships with a card: meaning, measured precision and recall, coverage, freshness, approved and disallowed uses, and an owner. Cards sit next to the tables downstream teams already query.
solutions.precedent: Model Cards (Mitchell et al., 2019); Datasheets for Datasets (Gebru et al., 2018)

solutions.name: Usage telemetry with risk flags
solutions.description: Log which teams read which attributes for which surface, and flag risky patterns such as an unverified attribute driving a hard filter.
solutions.precedent: OpenLineage and Marquez lineage capture; Snowflake ACCESS_HISTORY

solutions.name: Semantic layer that returns quality with the value
solutions.description: Downstream reads go through an interface that returns each value with confidence, verification status, and freshness, and refuses disallowed uses. Teams stop reading raw tables.
solutions.precedent: dbt Semantic Layer (MetricFlow); Open Data Contract Standard (Bitol)

demonstrate.idea: Every claim in the gluten-free engine's API carries status, confidence, sources, and last-checked date, and the demo shows a downstream filter using status correctly.
A mock data product card page for five attributes showing precision, coverage, freshness, and allowed uses.
An MCP server over the engine where the server refuses to assert 'safe for celiac' unless the status is Verified, demonstrated with a live agent.

painpoints.title: Attributes were modeled as product page badges, and agents need something else
painpoints.summary: Historically, any attribute catalog created became a badge on the product detail page. Agentic shopping through Clementine and partners such as OpenAI needs attributes that mean something different, and the team is just starting to learn those data needs. Brittany said AI will force a rethink of the underlying data structure, and Peggy tied agentic shopping directly to more data needs.
painpoints.why_it_matters: Instacart's CTO has said the same catalog powers every surface. If an attribute only makes sense as a badge, agents will misuse it or skip it.

sources.quote: any attribute we create now becomes a badge on the product detail page. And that's what an attribute is.
sources.context: Explaining pain points after Mike asked about diagnostics. Labeled 'Them'.

sources.quote: what an attribute means for agentic shopping is very different than what an attribute means for what's shown on a PDP page.
sources.context: Same answer, continued.

sources.quote: Partner called Clementine as well as integrations with OpenAI and starting to see how is that the same and different from how they shop Instacart. And what data needs are there?
sources.context: Mike asked about the 12-month outlook for the catalog PM.

sources.quote: in the world of AI, it's going to force us to rethink ... the underlying infrastructure and data structure for how we store that information.
sources.context: Describing the first six months of the role.

sources.quote: Now with agentic shopping, we have this Clementine, which is a kind of internal agentic shopping experience, which equates to more data needs.
sources.context: What she looks for in a PM partner.

sources.quote: do we have to do that with the changing needs of our data and, like, AI and agentic?
sources.context: On when to re-architect.

solutions.name: Separate assertion from presentation
solutions.description: Store each attribute as a typed assertion with evidence and confidence, and derive badges, filters, and agent facts as views over it. The product page stops dictating the schema.
solutions.precedent: Schema.org Product properties; Wikidata statements with references and ranks

solutions.name: Learn agent data needs from query logs
solutions.description: Cluster Clementine and partner queries to find the attribute questions agents ask that catalog cannot answer, and rank new attributes by unanswered demand.
solutions.precedent: Zero-result query analytics in Algolia and Elasticsearch

solutions.name: Agent-facing catalog contract
solutions.description: Define what an agent may assert about a product (verified, claimed, unknown) and expose it through a tool interface that requires uncertainty language.
solutions.precedent: Model Context Protocol; Agentic Commerce Protocol from OpenAI and Stripe (Instacart's ChatGPT app uses it per its public release)

demonstrate.idea: Show the same gluten-free evidence rendered two ways: as a PDP badge and as an agent tool response with status and caveats.
Write 100 realistic dietary agent prompts and score which ones the current public attribute set can answer.
An MCP server over the evidence engine plus a Claude agent that builds a celiac-safe cart and explains each item's evidence.

painpoints.title: Shipped pipelines need refresh, audits, and monitoring
painpoints.summary: Catalog is a data product, so maintenance never ends. Data has to be refreshed, AI pipelines need ongoing audits and quality monitoring, and every shipped attribute generates escalations. With hundreds of pipelines live, Peggy said the best PMs think about that maintenance at scale alongside building new.
painpoints.why_it_matters: Products get reformulated and labels change, so a correct tag decays. Unmonitored pipelines drift quietly until a customer finds the error.

sources.quote: data has to get refreshed, right? We might have to do ongoing audits or monitor the quality of all our AI pipelines.
sources.context: What she looks for in a PM partner.

sources.quote: If we just continue to build the new, then we'll continue to get escalations on the stuff we've already shipped and maintained. And catalog being a data product means that maintenance is always top of mind.
sources.context: Same answer, continued.

sources.quote: her team creates now hundreds of these pipelines.
sources.context: Describing Peggy's team. Labeled 'Them'.

solutions.name: Refresh cadence per attribute
solutions.description: Give each attribute a time-to-live based on how fast the truth changes, and re-verify on expiry or on UPC and label change signals.
solutions.precedent: GS1 GDSN item change notifications; HTTP cache TTL semantics

solutions.name: Pipeline observability
solutions.description: Track volume, distribution shift, confidence mix, and override rate per pipeline, and alert on anomalies.
solutions.precedent: Monte Carlo and Soda data observability; Great Expectations

solutions.name: Continuous re-verification from the field
solutions.description: Use shopper photos and shelf video to re-read labels of high-risk items on a rolling basis and diff them against stored claims.
solutions.precedent: DoorDash Dasher in-store photo capture for attribute extraction (DoorDash engineering blog); Instacart's Arpalus acquisition (2026)

demonstrate.idea: Give each claim in the gluten-free engine a last-verified date and an expiry, and show what expires this week.
A drift monitor: rerun extraction monthly on Open Food Facts updates and chart which claims changed.
Simulate field re-verification by feeding new label photos through the LLM reader and flagging reformulated products automatically.

painpoints.title: Subjective health claims need definitions and legal sign-off
painpoints.summary: Diet tags can be subjective and their terminology shifts over time. For a GLP-1 attribute, Peggy said the business is interested but legal is asking whether Instacart should do it at all and how to show it the right way.

sources.quote: Some of it can mean similar things or maybe the terminology of what's a diet tag. Diet changes it can be subjective.

solutions.name: Claim definition review
solutions.description: Legal, nutrition, product, and ops approve a written definition, scoring rule, and display language before any subjective attribute ships.
solutions.precedent: FDA final rule updating the 'healthy' nutrient content claim (Dec 2024); Instacart's public Health Tag definitions

solutions.name: Show objective facts and let the user set the filter
solutions.description: For GLP-1, surface protein per serving, fiber, and portion size as facts with a user-set filter, and skip any 'GLP-1 friendly' endorsement.

solutions.name: Externally owned claim standard
solutions.description: Co-develop a claim standard with a clinical or certifying body and license the mark, so the definition has an outside owner.

Extend the engine with a facts-only GLP-1 view computed from USDA FoodData Central nutrients, with no endorsement badge.
A versioned claim-definition service: change the gluten-free definition and watch which products change status, with an approval trail.

painpoints.title: The same incidents recur because fixes stay symptomatic
painpoints.summary: Sonali saw the same issue resurface as a new incident three or four months apart, because the real fix required changing the architecture. Tarang said Instacart writes the equivalent of COEs but tends to take short-term action items, where at Amazon a bad COE rebaselined the roadmap. Sonali also wanted crisper ownership and runbooks.
painpoints.why_it_matters: Repeat incidents cost twice and erode the trust leadership extends to catalog for bigger bets. Sonali said enough investment has not been made.

sources.quote: simple things like we were literally, I feel like, three, four months apart, have the same issue bubble up as a different incident.
